threads.thread_goal: Align on current-state process map and main pain points.

messages.text:
Sharing the first draft of the current-state intake and handover flow for the integrated service lane project_title: Integrated Service Lane for Vehicle Sales and Workshop.
I have mapped from first contact (walk-in or phone) through to workshop handover based on what we do today and added it into A1, linked back to T1.
Key steps I captured:
- Sales or service desk greeting and basic details
- Informal assessment of whether it is sales, service, or both
- Paper job card creation
- Keys and vehicle movement to the back
- Verbal handover to whoever is free in the workshop
Before we move on, I would like everyone to check if this reflects reality on the ground, especially around how information moves between sales and workshop.
Please comment on anything missing or wrong, and also call out the biggest pain points you see so we can prioritise later.

Thanks for putting A1 together.
From the workshop side, a couple of details I see daily that might not be fully captured:
- When sales books a service during a vehicle sale, the notes they add are often very short. That means when the car actually arrives, we have to call the customer again to clarify the complaint.
- For electrical issues, we usually need more detail (warning lights, when it happens, any previous work). Right now that is rarely written on the job card.
Also, there is an informal step where technicians quickly look over the car in the lane before moving it to a bay, mainly for safety (tyres, leaks, obvious damage). I do not see that explicitly in A1.
I would mark these as pain points: missing technical detail at handover and no structured intake check.

Looking at A1 from my side on the lane, I agree with most of the steps.
Two things I would add:
- Sometimes customers come straight to the workshop door instead of the front desk. Then we do a quick talk with them and only later send them back to sales or service desk for paperwork.
- When we position vehicles for maintenance and repair, we often discover extra issues (for example, brake noise, worn tyres) but there is no clear place in the current flow to record that before work starts.
Pain points I see:
1) Customers not always going through a single entry point.
2) Extra findings not consistently written down, which later causes confusion about what was agreed with the customer.

From the sales floor side, A1 looks close, but I think we should show two slightly different paths:
- One where the customer is buying a car and we book first service or accessories fitting at the same time.
- Another where the customer only needs service or repair.
Right now, when I identify customer needs during a sale, I usually just write short notes on the order form and then later someone copies part of that into the job card. That copy step is slow and we sometimes lose details.
Pain points from my view:
- Double entry of customer and vehicle data.
- No standard way to capture technical complaints when I am the first contact.
Not sure if that should be in A1 as separate branches or just notes.

I walked through A1 and compared it with how we actually move cars and assign bays.
What I notice:
- The current map shows bay assignment as a single step, but in practice we decide based on who is free, not on job type. That leads to urgent or warranty jobs waiting behind routine work.
- There is no explicit step for checking parts availability before we move the car into a bay.
I would add these as process gaps and pain points:
1) No clear rule for urgent or warranty prioritisation.
2) Cars sometimes occupy bays while we wait for parts.
This will be important later when we work on T4, but it should already appear in the current-state view so we do not forget it.

Good points from both of you.
I will update A1 to:
- Add an explicit quick visual and safety check in the lane before bay assignment.
- Show the informal calls back to customers when job card information is incomplete.
- Mark the branch where customers go straight to the workshop door and then get redirected.
Once I update the map, I will re-share so we can confirm it is accurate before we lock it as the baseline for T1.
Meanwhile, can we list all pain points mentioned so far and see if anything is missing?

Let me summarise the pain points I heard and add one more from my side:
- Missing technical detail when sales or front desk creates the job card.
- No structured intake check in the lane.
- Customers entering through multiple doors.
- Extra findings during positioning not consistently recorded.
- Double entry of customer and vehicle data.
- No clear rule for urgent or warranty prioritisation.
- Cars blocking bays while waiting for parts.
I would also add: customers often do not get a clear expectation on intake time and when we will call them back. That leads to follow-up calls and complaints.
We can later choose the top three for the pilot focus as part of D2.

On the customer expectation point, I agree.
When I book service during a sale, I usually give a rough idea of timing, but when the car actually comes in weeks later, the workshop schedule is different. There is no link between what I promised and what the lane can actually handle.
For the pilot, I think we should focus on:
- Better handover information from sales to workshop.
- Clearer intake communication to the customer.
Not sure if the bay allocation rules should be in the top three or just behind those.

From a supervision point of view, if we do not tackle bay allocation and parts waiting, the lane will still feel blocked even if the handover is better.
My suggestion for D2 later would be:
1) Improve sales-to-workshop handover quality.
2) Introduce a structured intake and triage check in the lane.
3) Define basic bay allocation and prioritisation rules.
Customer communication will improve as a result of the first two, but we can also add a simple script without making it a separate top pain point.
Open to adjusting this if others see it differently.

I like that list.
From the lane, the structured intake and triage check will help us a lot with safety and quick diagnostics. If we combine that with better handover information, we will spend less time chasing details.
For bay allocation, even a simple rule like urgent and warranty first, then routine, would already be a big step.
So I support those three as the main focus for D2.

I have now updated A1 with the extra branches and steps we discussed:
- Separate entry points for sales-led bookings and direct service visits.
- Explicit quick safety and visual check in the lane.
- Informal callbacks to customers when information is missing.
- Note about cars waiting in bays for parts.
Unless anyone spots a major gap, I suggest we treat this as the final current-state map for T1 and move on to designing the future flow.
Please shout if there is any missing step that would change how we design the pilot.

I checked the updated A1 and from what I see on the ground it matches our current reality.
The only thing I will keep an eye on is how often customers bypass the front desk, but that is already shown as a branch.
From my side, we can close T1 on the mapping part.

I have also reviewed A1 focusing on the sales and booking steps.
The two paths you added (sale plus future service, and direct service) look right to me. The double entry of data is visible, which is good for later.
I am comfortable using this as our baseline map for the project.

From the supervision and bay allocation side, the updated A1 reflects how we currently assign work and where we get blocked.
I agree with closing the current-state mapping and moving on to the design tasks T2, T3, and T4.
On the pain point priorities for D2, I still support the three I listed earlier unless someone wants to swap one out.

Let us close D2 so we can brief the design work clearly.
Based on the discussion, I propose the top three pain points we will address in the pilot design are:
1) Incomplete or low-quality sales-to-workshop handover information.
2) Lack of a structured intake and triage check in the lane.
3) No clear bay allocation and prioritisation rules, leading to blocked capacity.
Customer communication at intake will be improved as part of the first two.
If there are no objections, we will use these three to guide T2, T3, and T4.

No objections from me.
Those three pain points match what I see every day in the lane and in the workshop.
Happy to support on T3 when we start drafting the intake and triage checklist.

Agreed on the three priorities.
They cover the main causes of rework and delays we have been dealing with.
I will keep notes from the lane to feed into T3 and later into A3.

I am aligned with those three pain points.
For T2, I will focus the handover form and script on capturing the technical details and customer expectations that you highlighted.
We can review a first draft together in the next thread.

threads.thread_goal: Define the new intake workflow, handover form, and triage checklist.

messages.text:
As agreed in TH1, I have drafted the new sales-to-workshop handover form and intake script and added them into A2, linked to T2.
Structure of the form:
- Customer and vehicle details (to avoid double entry later).
- Reason for visit, with guided questions for symptoms (warning lights, noises, when it happens, previous work).
- Customer expectations (wait, leave car, preferred contact, budget indication).
- Safety notes and visible damage.
The script mirrors the form so that we can follow it in person or on the phone.
Sharing here for feedback, especially from the workshop and supervision side, before we lock the mandatory fields for D3.

I went through A2 with a workshop lens.
Positive points:
- The symptom questions will really help for electrical and intermittent issues.
- Capturing previous work on the same problem is important for warranty.
Suggestions:
- Add a field for dashboard warning lights with options (engine, ABS, airbag, etc.).
- Include a checkbox for whether the customer has left any personal items in the car, to avoid disputes.
For D3, I would consider the following as mandatory fields: vehicle identification, main complaint description, symptom details, previous related work, and customer contact preference.

From my side, A2 already covers most of what I usually have to ask again at the lane.
One more detail that would help the triage checklist later: a simple field for whether the issue is safety-critical from the customer point of view (for example, brakes, steering, tyres). Even if their judgement is not perfect, it helps us prioritise.
Also, could we add a small section for known modifications or accessories (tow bar, aftermarket electronics)? That often affects diagnostics.
These would feed nicely into A3 when we build the intake and triage checklist under T3.

Looking at A2 from a coordination angle, I like that it already includes customer expectations and preferred contact.
To connect with T4 later, I suggest we add a simple job type classification on the form: urgent safety, warranty, routine service, diagnostic only, accessories.
This will allow us to apply bay allocation rules more easily.
For D3, I would make job type classification mandatory as well, otherwise the triage in the lane will still be guesswork.

Thanks for the draft, this is a good step.
From a customer and operations view, I want to keep the form usable at the front desk and on the sales floor.
Two checks:
- Can we keep the number of mandatory fields limited so that intake time stays under the 20-minute target?
- Are all fields compatible with our existing system, or do we need a paper add-on for some items?
For D3, I would like us to agree on a core set of mandatory fields that we can realistically capture every time, and mark the rest as recommended.

Good point on intake time.
I checked against our current system screens. Most of the customer and vehicle fields already exist. The new parts are mainly the symptom guidance, safety-critical flag, job type classification, and personal items note.
Proposal for D3 mandatory fields:
- Customer and vehicle identification.
- Main complaint description.
- Symptom details (structured questions).
- Job type classification.
- Customer contact preference.
The rest (previous work, modifications, personal items, safety-critical flag) can be recommended but not strictly mandatory.
If we agree, I will update A2 accordingly.

I can work with that list.
Even if previous work and safety-critical flag are not mandatory, we can emphasise them in training so they are used most of the time.
From the lane side, as long as we always get the main complaint, symptom details, and job type, we can build a solid triage in A3.
So I support your proposal for D3.

Agreed from my side as well.
Those mandatory fields will already reduce a lot of back-and-forth.
When we design the triage checklist under T3, we can reference these fields directly so technicians know where to look on the form.

I am fine with that mandatory set.
Job type classification being mandatory is the key link to T4 and later to A5.
Let us lock D3 with that structure so we can move on to the triage checklist and the new lane workflow.

Understood, I will update A2 with the agreed mandatory and recommended fields and mark T2 as ready for validation.
Switching to the triage checklist: @247886 shared a first draft of A3 linked to T3.
Could you summarise the main steps here so we can review and then close D4 on the triage flow?

Sure, here is the structure of the triage checklist in A3 for T3:
1) Safety and basic checks in the lane: leaks, tyre condition, lights, warning messages, obvious damage, personal items.
2) Confirm complaint and symptom details with the customer or from A2, correcting anything unclear.
3) Quick functional checks based on job type (for example, brake pedal feel for brake jobs, battery test for electrical complaints).
4) Documentation: record findings, note any extra work suggested, and confirm with customer before proceeding.
5) Bay assignment suggestion based on job type and estimated time, to feed into T4 and A5.
Timing-wise, the goal is to keep this triage under 10 minutes per vehicle so we stay within the 20-minute intake target overall.

I like the structure.
One practical suggestion: in step 3, maybe we can group the quick checks into a short list per job type so technicians do not have to think from scratch each time.
For example, for routine service: fluid levels, visible leaks, tyre wear, lights. For electrical: battery test, check fuses, scan for codes if available.
That will help keep the triage within the 10-minute target.

From a coordination point of view, I want to make sure the triage output is clear enough for bay allocation.
Could we add a simple triage outcome field at the end of A3: ready for bay, needs parts check first, needs customer decision, or safety do not move?
This will connect directly into the lane workflow and A5 under T4.
If we include that, I am comfortable approving the steps and timing for D4.

Good idea.
I will add that triage outcome field to A3 and also group the quick checks by job type as @20895 suggested.
With those adjustments, the checklist will still fit on one page and should be practical to use in the lane.
From my side, the steps and timing are ready to be approved for D4.

Let us close D4.
We will adopt the triage checklist in A3 with the following structure:
- Safety and basic checks in the lane.
- Confirmation of complaint and symptom details using A2.
- Short, job-type-based quick checks.
- Documentation of findings and customer confirmation.
- Triage outcome (ready for bay, parts check first, customer decision, safety do not move).
Target triage time is under 10 minutes per vehicle.
This will feed into the new lane workflow and bay allocation rules in T4 and A5.

All clear from my side.
I will align the intake script in A2 with the triage steps in A3 so that the questions flow naturally from sales or front desk to the lane.
With D3 and D4 closed, T2 and T3 are ready for training preparation later.

threads.thread_goal: Lock in lane capacity rules, staff rota, and pilot schedule.

messages.text:
I have drafted the lane capacity rules and the staff rota for the pilot and added them into A5 and A8, linked to T5 and T8.
Key points:
- Pilot proposal: start in two weeks, run for 10 working days.
- Lane capacity: target of 4 intake slots per hour, with a maximum of 2 triage cases in progress at the same time.
- Bay allocation rules in A5: urgent safety and warranty first, then routine service, then diagnostics and accessories.
- Rota in A8: one dedicated intake technician per shift, one backup technician during peaks, and clear time blocks for sellers to handle intake using A2.
Please review and comment, especially on whether the capacity assumptions are realistic and if the rota covers peak times properly, before we close D5 and D6.

I checked A5 and A8.
On capacity: 4 intake slots per hour with triage under 10 minutes seems achievable if we avoid long conversations at the front.
On rota: the dedicated intake technician per shift is good, but I notice that on late afternoons we only have the backup technician for one hour. That is usually when customers rush in after work.
Suggestion: extend the backup technician coverage by one more hour in the afternoon, even if that means slightly less time on other tasks.
For D5, I am comfortable with the proposed start in two weeks and 10 working days duration, as long as we confirm training dates for T6 and T7 beforehand.

From the lane side, the capacity numbers look tight but manageable if we stick to the triage checklist in A3.
I agree with @118321 that late afternoon is a risk. That is when we see more walk-ins and people wanting to wait.
Could we also define an overflow rule in A5: if more than 2 triage cases are waiting, we temporarily redirect routine jobs to standard bays without full triage, just basic safety checks?
That would help avoid long queues in the lane.

Looking at A8, I see I am scheduled as intake technician on three mornings and two afternoons during the pilot.
That is fine for me, but we should make sure there is time blocked for cleaning the lane and checking safety items, not only triage.
Maybe we can add a short daily slot in the rota for lane housekeeping so it does not get forgotten.
On the pilot start date, two weeks from now gives us enough time to get used to A2 and A3.

From the sales side, A8 shows two sellers covering intake blocks in the morning and one in the afternoon.
Afternoons are usually busier for test drives and new sales, so I am a bit concerned about having only one seller available for intake then.
Could we shift one of the morning intake blocks to the afternoon, or at least have a flexible slot that we can move based on bookings?
For D5, I am ok with the pilot start in two weeks, but I will need to plan T6 training sessions next week to avoid clashes with peak sales times.

Good feedback.
I will adjust A8 to:
- Extend backup technician coverage by one extra hour in the late afternoon.
- Move one seller intake block from morning to afternoon, and mark one additional block as flexible depending on bookings.
- Add a 15-minute lane housekeeping slot at the start of each shift for the intake technician.
On overflow, I like @247886 suggestion. I will add to A5 that if more than 2 triage cases are waiting, routine jobs can be sent to standard bays with only basic safety checks.
With these changes, are we comfortable confirming D5: pilot start in two weeks, duration 10 working days?

With those rota and rule adjustments in A5 and A8, I am comfortable confirming D5.
Two weeks gives us time to complete T6 and T7 and to brief the team on the overflow rule.
I will also prepare a short visual of the bay allocation logic from A5 to post in the workshop.

Agreed on D5 from my side.
The overflow rule in A5 will be important to explain clearly to technicians so they know when to skip full triage.
I can help during T7 training to walk through a few examples.

I am ok with the pilot start and duration.
The updated A8 with more afternoon coverage should balance sales and intake better.
I will schedule T6 sessions for the sales team next week so everyone is ready before go-live.

From the lane, the adjusted rota in A8 looks workable.
The housekeeping slot will help keep the area safe and organised.
I am aligned with D5 and ready to support during the pilot.

Great, D5 is confirmed: pilot starts in two weeks and runs for 10 working days.
Let us now close D6 on the final rota and bay allocation rules.
To summarise A5 and A8 after changes:
- Bay allocation priority: urgent safety, warranty, routine service, diagnostics, accessories.
- Overflow: if more than 2 triage cases are waiting, routine jobs go to standard bays with basic safety checks only.
- Rota: dedicated intake technician each shift, extended backup coverage in late afternoons, adjusted seller intake blocks with one flexible slot, daily lane housekeeping slot.
If there are no further objections, we will treat A5 and A8 as final for the pilot.

No further changes from me.
The rules and rota as summarised match what we discussed and should be clear enough for the team.
I support closing D6 with A5 and A8 as the reference for the pilot.

Aligned on D6.
I will make sure technicians understand the priority order and overflow rule from A5 during T7.

threads.thread_goal: Monitor pilot progress, surface issues, and adjust quickly.

messages.text:
First day of the pilot is complete.
I have added initial KPI data into A4 and logged incidents under T9.
Headline numbers:
- Average intake time: 18 minutes (target under 20).
- 3 cases where triage exceeded 15 minutes.
- 2 safety near-misses in the lane (both related to customers walking into the triage area).
- 4 callbacks to clarify complaints despite using A2.
No major warranty or safety non-compliance found so far, but we will confirm against A6 as part of T11.
Please share what you observed today and any quick tweaks you think we should make this week, so we can decide on D7.

From the lane side, the triage checklist in A3 worked well overall.
Observations:
- The three long triage cases were complex electrical issues where we tried to do too much diagnosis in the lane instead of moving to a bay.
- The safety near-misses happened when customers followed their cars into the triage area. The floor markings are not very visible.
Quick tweaks I suggest:
1) For complex electrical complaints, limit lane triage to basic checks and move the car to a bay sooner.
2) Add a simple barrier or cone at the edge of the triage area and ask customers to wait at a marked spot.
These changes should keep us within the 10-minute triage target and improve safety.

I agree with @247886.
On the callbacks: in two of the four cases, the handover form in A2 had very short descriptions like engine noise without symptom details filled in.
Maybe we need to reinforce during intake that the guided questions are not optional.
Also, I noticed that during peak time we skipped the personal items and modifications fields to save time. That did not cause issues today, but it could later.
For D7, I would support a tweak to emphasise full use of the symptom section in A2 and to set a clear rule on what can be skipped only when the lane is overloaded.

From the sales and front desk side, the new script in A2 felt longer at first, but after a few customers it became smoother.
Where we struggled:
- When there is a queue, it is tempting to skip some of the symptom questions.
- Some colleagues are still using old habits and not following the script fully.
I propose a quick huddle tomorrow morning to remind everyone which fields in A2 are mandatory and why, and maybe share one or two examples from today where missing details caused callbacks.
That should help reduce rework without changing the form itself.

I reviewed the incidents log under T9 and did a quick check against A6 for safety.
Findings:
- The two near-misses are clearly about customer movement, not about vehicle handling or PPE.
- All documented steps for safety and warranty in A6 were followed in the cases I sampled.
I support the idea of adding a physical barrier and clearer waiting area markings.
On capacity, A4 shows that late afternoon is still the tightest period, but the overflow rule in A5 was used twice and worked as intended.
For D7, I would suggest we adopt the small safety and triage scope tweaks now and keep monitoring the KPIs daily.

Thanks for the detailed inputs.
Let me summarise the proposed tweaks so we can decide on D7:
- Limit lane triage for complex electrical issues to basic checks, then move to a bay.
- Add a simple barrier or cone and a marked waiting area for customers to reduce lane access.
- Reinforce use of mandatory symptom fields in A2 via a short huddle and examples.
- Clarify which non-mandatory fields can be skipped only when the lane is overloaded, not by default.
None of these changes affect the core workflow, so they fit within the pilot scope.
If we agree, we will implement them from tomorrow and continue tracking in A4 and T9.

That summary matches what I had in mind.
I can take care of adjusting the triage practice for complex electrical cases and help set up the cones and waiting area tomorrow morning.
I support adopting these tweaks as part of D7.

Agreed.
I will remind technicians during the shift change about the new limit on electrical triage in the lane and the importance of using the symptom details from A2.
These are small changes but should help keep intake times under control and improve safety.

I am on board.
I will run a short huddle with the sales and front desk team tomorrow to reinforce the mandatory fields in A2 and share the callback examples.
We will also remind customers where to wait while their car is in triage.
Happy to have these tweaks recorded under D7.

Aligned with the tweaks.
I will update the safety checklist in A6 to mention the customer waiting area explicitly and note the new practice in the T11 review.
We can then check at the end of the week if near-misses have dropped in A4.

Thanks all.
We will record D7 as: implement limited triage for complex electrical issues, introduce a physical and visual separation for the customer waiting area, and reinforce mandatory use of symptom fields in A2, with clear guidance on when optional fields can be skipped.
These changes take effect from tomorrow and will be monitored via A4 and T9.
Please keep logging any new issues so we can adjust again if needed.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results, customer feedback, and next steps.

messages.text:
Pilot period is complete.
I have uploaded a draft pilot report under T12 and updated A4 with final KPIs. Customer feedback from T10 is summarised in A7.
Headline results:
- Average intake time over the pilot: 17 minutes (better than target).
- Rework cases due to poor handover dropped by about 40 percent compared to baseline.
- Customer callbacks about unclear complaints reduced from 8 per week to 3 per week.
- Two minor safety incidents early on, none after we introduced the waiting area tweak from D7.
Customer feedback in A7 is mostly positive about clarity and speed, with some comments about waiting area comfort.
We now need to decide under D8 whether to roll out the integrated lane process permanently and what improvements to implement before full rollout.

From the lane perspective, the new process with A2, A3, and A5 felt much more structured than before.
What worked well:
- Triage checklist in A3 made safety checks consistent.
- Bay allocation rules in A5 reduced situations where urgent jobs were stuck behind routine work.
- Overflow rule helped during the busiest afternoons.
Areas to improve before full rollout:
- Some technicians still forget to record extra findings and customer confirmations on the checklist.
- The physical waiting area could use clearer signage and maybe a small barrier that is more visible.
I would support rolling out permanently, with a focus on reinforcing documentation habits and improving the waiting area setup.

I agree with @247886.
On a day-to-day basis, the lane felt more predictable. We spent less time chasing information and more time actually working on cars.
From my notes:
- The 10-minute triage target was realistic once we got used to the checklist.
- The main delays now come from parts availability, which is outside the intake process itself.
Before full rollout, I would like to see a short refresher session for technicians on documentation and customer communication at intake, maybe as part of T7 follow-up.
Overall, I am in favour of making the integrated lane the standard way of working.

Looking at A7, customers appreciated that we explained what would happen next and when they would hear from us.
From the sales and front desk side:
- The intake script in A2 is now familiar and does not slow us down.
- The main challenge is keeping everyone consistent, especially new or temporary staff.
Suggestions before full rollout:
- Create a short one-page guide or quick reference for A2 that we can keep at the desk.
- Include the integrated lane process in onboarding for new sellers and service advisors.
With those in place, I support rolling out the process permanently.

From a supervision and coordination view, the pilot showed clear benefits:
- The bay allocation rules in A5 reduced idle time and made priorities visible.
- The rota in A8 worked well after the adjustments; we rarely had more than 2 triage cases waiting.
- Safety compliance against A6 was good after the D7 tweaks.
For improvements before full rollout:
- We should formalise a monthly review of A2, A3, and A5 to keep them up to date.
- It would help to add a simple parts readiness check step into the workflow, even if it is just a reminder.
I recommend we roll out the integrated lane as the standard, with these governance and minor process additions.

Thanks for the inputs.
Let me summarise the proposal for D8:
- Roll out the integrated lane process permanently, using A2, A3, A5, and A8 as standard references.
- Before full rollout, implement the following improvements:
  - Reinforce technician documentation and customer communication via a short refresher (extension of T7).
  - Create a one-page quick reference for the intake script in A2 and include it in T6 materials.
  - Improve waiting area signage and barrier visibility.
  - Add a simple parts readiness reminder step into the workflow.
  - Set up a monthly review of A2, A3, and A5 to keep them current.
If everyone agrees, we will document this in the final T12 report and plan the rollout schedule.

That summary matches what I saw during the pilot.
I support rolling out the integrated lane permanently with those improvements.
I can help with the technician refresher and with defining the parts readiness reminder in the triage flow.

Agreed on D8.
The integrated lane has made our work more organised and safer.
I will support with examples and tips during the technician refresher so that documentation becomes a habit.

I am aligned with rolling out the process permanently.
I will prepare the one-page quick reference for A2 and update T6 materials so that new and existing sellers have a clear guide.
Customer feedback in A7 supports this direction.

I also support D8.
I will work with you to define the monthly review routine for A2, A3, and A5 and to include the parts readiness reminder in the workflow.
These steps will help keep the process effective over time.

Thanks everyone.
We will record D8 as: roll out the integrated lane process permanently, with the agreed improvements on training, quick references, waiting area setup, parts readiness reminder, and monthly document reviews.
I will finalise the T12 report to reflect this decision and propose a rollout timeline to our leadership for confirmation.
Please keep A4 and A7 handy as references when we present the results.
